questions.title: Be Curious · What do you notice? What do you wonder?
questions.hint: Compare each shaded rectangle with the red 15 × 12 rectangle.
steps: Notice which rectangles are bigger or smaller than the red one, and which is closest.
questions.answer: Sample answer: I notice each teal rectangle uses rounded numbers to estimate 15 × 12 = 180. 20 × 10 = 200 and 15 × 10 = 150 are close; 20 × 12 = 240 is too big because both factors were rounded up. I wonder which way of rounding gives the closest estimate.
questions.verification: Computed 15×12=180, 20×10=200, 15×10=150, 20×12=240 in Python; compared with the drawn rectangles.

questions.title: Math is… Mindset
questions.hint: Think about what you do first when a word problem looks confusing.
steps: Think of a time a math situation was hard to understand.
Write what helped you, like drawing a picture or rounding the numbers.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Drawing a picture and estimating first helps me make sense of a situation. Your answer may be different.
questions.verification: Reflection prompt; no single correct answer.

questions.title: Learn · Money from 432 tickets at $13
questions.hint: Multiply the number of people by the ticket price, using friendly numbers.
steps: The real answer, $5,616, is between the two estimates, so it makes sense.
questions.answer: About $4,300 to $6,000. The exact amount is 432 × 13 = $5,616.
questions.verification: Computed 432×13=5,616, 400×15=6,000, 430×10=4,300 in Python; 5,616 lies between the estimates.

questions.title: Math is… Choosing Tools
questions.hint: An estimate tells you 'about how much', not 'exactly how much'.
steps: Think about what an estimate is close to.
Think about what it cannot tell you exactly.
questions.answer: Sample answer: An estimate tells me about how big the answer should be, so I can check if my answer is reasonable. It can't tell me the exact answer.
questions.verification: Reflection prompt; answer checked against the Learn example.

questions.title: Work Together · 879 × 36
questions.hint: Round each factor to a number that is easy to multiply.
steps: Explain why you picked your strategy.
questions.answer: One possible answer: 900 × 40 = 36,000 (rounded factors), because those numbers are easy to multiply. Compatible numbers 900 × 35 = 31,500 are also reasonable. The exact product is 31,644.
questions.verification: Computed 879×36=31,644, 900×40=36,000, 900×35=31,500 in Python; both estimates are near the exact product.

questions.title: Problem 1 · 643 × 18
questions.hint: Round each factor to its greatest place value.
questions.answer: About 12,000 (600 × 20). Other close estimates are fine. (Exact: 11,574.)
questions.verification: Computed 643×18=11,574 and 600×20=12,000 in Python; estimate is close to the exact product.

questions.title: Problem 2 · 325 × 62
questions.hint: Round each factor to its greatest place value.
questions.answer: About 18,000 (300 × 60). Compatible numbers 325 × 60 = 19,500 is even closer. Other close estimates are fine. (Exact: 20,150.)
questions.verification: Computed 325×62=20,150 and 300×60=18,000 in Python; estimate is close to the exact product.

questions.title: Problem 3 · 438 × 27
questions.hint: Round each factor to its greatest place value.
questions.answer: About 12,000 (400 × 30). Other close estimates are fine. (Exact: 11,826.)
questions.verification: Computed 438×27=11,826 and 400×30=12,000 in Python; estimate is close to the exact product.

questions.title: Problem 4 · 572 × 49
questions.hint: Round each factor to its greatest place value.
questions.answer: About 30,000 (600 × 50). Other close estimates are fine. (Exact: 28,028.)
questions.verification: Computed 572×49=28,028 and 600×50=30,000 in Python; estimate is close to the exact product.

questions.answer: About $4,800 (400 × 12). 400 × 10 = $4,000 is also a reasonable estimate. (Exact: $4,860.)

questions.title: 9 · Han's error
questions.hint: Make your own estimate of 492 × 32 and compare it with 1,200.
steps: Compare: 1,200 is much too small, so Han's estimate is not reasonable.
questions.answer: Han is not correct. 492 × 32 is about 500 × 30 = 15,000, so 1,200 is far too small (he may have lost zeros). (Exact: 15,744.)
questions.verification: Computed 492×32=15,744 and 500×30=15,000 in Python; 1,200 is about 13 times too small.

questions.title: Problem 10 · Estimate for 658 × 19
questions.hint: Round each factor and see which equation matches.
steps: 19 is very close to 20, so the estimate should use 20.
650 × 20 = 13,000. A and C use 10, which is too far from 19.
questions.answer: B. 650 × 20 = 13,000, because 650 and 20 are both close to 658 and 19. (Exact: 12,502.)
questions.verification: Computed 658×19=12,502 and each option in Python; only B (13,000) is close.

questions.title: Problem 11 · Rounded or compatible?
questions.hint: Try both strategies on 246 × 38 and compare the results.
steps: Rounded: 246 rounds to 200 and 38 rounds to 40, so 200 × 40 = 8,000.
Compatible: 246 is close to 250, and 250 × 40 = 10,000 is easy (25 × 4 = 100).
questions.answer: One possible answer: Compatible numbers give the greater estimate. 250 × 40 = 10,000 is greater than the rounded 200 × 40 = 8,000, because 246 rounds down to 200 but goes up to 250 as a compatible number. (Exact: 9,348.)
questions.verification: Computed 246×38=9,348, 200×40=8,000, 250×40=10,000 in Python. Depends on the rounding chosen, so marked open-ended.

questions.title: 12 · Recycling club goal
questions.hint: Find the total bottles for one student first, or for one day.
steps: 8,750 is more than 8,000, so they met the goal.
questions.answer: About 8,750 bottles (25 × 70 × 5). Yes, they met their goal of 8,000. (Exact: 26 × 72 × 5 = 9,360.)
questions.verification: Computed 26×72×5=9,360 and 25×70×5=8,750 in Python; both exceed 8,000.

questions.title: Reflect · Is my product reasonable?
questions.hint: Think about how an estimate is like a target to compare against.
steps: Estimate first with rounded or compatible numbers.
If the exact product is close to the estimate, it is reasonable; if not, check your work.
questions.answer: Sample answer: I estimate the product first. If my calculated answer is close to my estimate, it is reasonable. If it is very far away, I made a mistake and should check again.
questions.verification: Reflection prompt; matches the lesson's Learn example (5,616 between 4,300 and 6,000).
